that in our blindness we have been insensitive to these smaller

I cannot myself say in detail-nor is it my duty to do so—
where and at what point God's summons hits the individual,
you and me, in the course of our daily life, in the routine
of our work and our many social contacts. For it is the
mystery of Jesus' encounter with us that He meets us dis-
guised in ever new forms; it is the mystery of God's call that
it comes to us always clad in a different shape, that it sounds
ever new, and in circumstances where we least expected it.
Hence I can give only a general warning that each of us
should be prepared and vigilant and alert both to hear the
summons and to obey it.
The popular legend of the poor and the rich man, which
no doubt is familiar to all of us, has as its basic presupposition
that God's meeting with man often takes unexpected forms
and that if we fail in vigilance we overlook it to our hurt.
The legend relates how God once walked the earth as a
simple wayfarer, and sought a shelter for the night. He
knocked at the door of a rich man and asked for sleeping
accommodation. The rich man looked at the unpromising
wayfarer who stood at his door, and whose appearance did
not exactly suggest that He would be able to pay well, and
on various pretexts he refused Him shelter. It was just not
convenient. God then knocked at the door of the poor man's
house, where He found a friendly reception. As the tale goes
on to say, the rich man had punished himself, whereas the
poor man was granted a rich blessing.
Yes, friendliness and kindheartedness, patience and the
will to sacrifice oneself are essential to the vigilance that is
required of us; perceptiveness about what the present
occasion demands. God comes to us, Jesus comes to us in
disguise; and if we have failed to recognize the encounter,
then the moment has irrevocably fled and we have missed
the blessing with which it was rich. Hence we should insert
